explain.say: Your eyes send the brain a flat, patchy picture. The brain turns it into a solid world by making quick, clever guesses, and an illusion is a picture that tricks those guesses.

faq.a: An optical illusion is a picture or scene that the brain sees differently from how it really is: lines look bent, colours look different, or still images seem to move. It happens because seeing is the brain interpreting signals, not just recording them.

faq.q: Why do squares of the same grey look like different shades?
faq.a: The brain knows shadows make things darker, so it brightens anything it thinks is in shadow. Two identical greys, one in apparent shadow, end up looking quite different.
asks: How does the checker shadow illusion work?
Why does the same colour look different?

faq.q: Why do two lines of the same length look different?
faq.a: In the Muller-Lyer illusion, arrow ends pointing outward or inward make one line look longer. One explanation is that the brain reads the ends like the corners of a room and wall, near or far, and adjusts the size.
asks: Why do arrow lines look longer?

faq.q: Why does the Moon look bigger near the horizon?
faq.a: The Moon's picture in your eye is the same size high up or low down. Near the horizon the brain compares it with trees and buildings and treats it as far away, so it seems larger. This is the Moon illusion.
asks: Is the Moon bigger when it rises?

faq.q: Do illusions mean my eyes are not working properly?
faq.a: No. Illusions fool almost everyone, because they use the same shortcuts that normally help the brain see quickly and correctly. They show how the brain works, not that it is broken.
asks: Are illusions a sign of bad eyesight?
Why does everyone fall for illusions?

facts: The Moon's image on the retina is the same size whether it is high in the sky or near the horizon.
The Muller-Lyer illusion, with arrow-shaped line ends, was described by Franz Carl Muller-Lyer in 1889.
